title: Fish a screw that slid under a circuit board out of an open chassis and into the magnetic parts dish
instruction: A screw has slid under the circuit board in this open chassis. Get it out and into the magnetic parts dish, then leave the pick-up tool back in its holder and the chassis back on its block, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Screws dropped into equipment while it is being assembled or repaired roll under boards and brackets where neither fingers nor tools reach. Technicians tip the unit to bring the screw out, and fish it out with a magnetic pick-up while holding the unit tipped, since the screw slides back as soon as it is set down.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) An open-topped equipment chassis, 1.2 kg: a 1.5 mm steel tray 26 cm long left to right, 16 cm deep, 3 cm tall (walls modelled 4 mm thick), its floor lined with a PTFE sheet (friction about 0.06 for the screw); its middle 30 cm forward and 6 cm left of the centre line. It stands on four rubber feet 14 mm square and 8 mm tall, 6 cm either side of its long axis and 11 cm either side of its middle; its right end's feet stand on a wooden block 20 x 4.5 cm and 2.3 cm tall, so its floor slopes 6 degrees down to the left. A green FR-4 circuit board 14.6 x 12.6 cm, 2 mm thick, covers the floor's left half on four steel M3 hex standoffs 5 mm across and 12 mm tall (a 12 mm gap over the floor), 1.2 cm in from the board's ends and 6.5 cm either side of its middle. A black plastic carrying handle stands over the left end's wall: two 8 mm square posts 9 cm apart and a 10 cm bar 16 mm square, 3 cm over the wall's top. (2) A zinc-plated M4 x 14 mm pan-head machine screw (head 8 mm across, 3.5 mm tall), 2.5 g, lying on its side under the circuit board, its axis front to back with the head to the back, in the middle of the floor 1.2 cm from the left end's wall. (3) A magnetic pick-up tool standing upright in a wooden holder (6 x 5.8 cm, 7.1 cm tall, a 3 x 2.8 cm pocket) 20 cm forward and 20 cm right of the centre line: a black rubber handle 3 cm tall (4 by 1.6 cm) resting across the pocket, a 6 mm steel rod 5.5 cm long and a red ferrite magnet 1.4 cm across and 1.2 cm tall at its foot; 60 g. (4) A dark steel magnetic parts dish, 9 cm across and 2 cm deep, 30 cm forward and 17 cm right of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 1.0 with the screw in the parts dish (its middle within 4.1 cm of the dish's middle, below the dish's rim), the pick-up tool back in its holder (within 3 cm of where it started), the chassis back down on its block (within 2 degrees and 2 cm of where it started), each gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) at least 4 cm from the tool's handle and from the chassis's handle, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5 with the screw in the dish; 0.25 if the tool's magnet has picked the screw up at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the screw, the tool and the chassis still.
reset_notes: Put the screw back under the circuit board at the left end, the tool back on its holder and the chassis back on its block.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control) at real size and mass. Simplified: the magnets are rules: the screw sticks to the tool's tip once the tip is within 2 cm of it (a real magnet needs closer, about 1 cm) and to the dish once touched into it; the screw slides on the PTFE-lined floor (friction 0.06), so it settles under the board at 6 degrees of slope and slides out when the chassis is tipped the other way. Cameras 1280 x 704.
